market: ES (traded as MES). Signal from ES's own prior RTH daily closes via the frozen bar['hist'] (roll-adjusted same-contract returns). ES chosen because the index-level evidence is for the S&P 500 and its futures.
hypothesis: A large prior L-day ES close-to-close return (L = 1 or 5 RTH sessions), scaled by 20-day daily return volatility, is partly reversed in the next RTH session: trading against it from 09:35 to 15:55 with a 1:1 bracket of 0.5 x ATR20 beats random-direction trades taken on the same sessions with the same bracket.
mechanism: Since ~2000 US index returns show NEGATIVE daily serial dependence (Baltussen, van Bekkum & Da 2019), linked to index products (futures/ETFs) and index arbitrage; Jones, Pyun & Wang (2016) find daily reversal in S&P 500 futures, strongest when implied variance is high and mostly after negative days. Liquidity-provision reading (Nagel 2012): index-level price pressure from flows that dealers absorb overnight is paid back by a partial reversal.

sources.summary: Baltussen, van Bekkum & Da (2019, JFE 132(1) 26-48), 'Indexing and stock market serial dependence around the world': across 20 indexes in 15 countries, daily AR(1) of index returns was positive until the 1990s and is negative since the 2000s (10-year average about -0.05 to -0.1 for MAC(5) by 2010-16). A strategy trading on MAC(5) after 1999 has an annual Sharpe of 0.63 (0.67 for the S&P 500 alone); futures and ETFs show similar negative dependence. Links it to index products and arbitrage. Gross of costs. Caveats: MAC(q) is a variance-ratio-style weighting of daily autocorrelations at lags 1..q-1, not a cumulative 5-day return, so L5 here is NOT their statistic; their strategy is close-to-close (includes the overnight, which this RTH trade misses); their sample ends 2016, so ES dev 2011-18 is mostly in-sample for the paper.

Jones, Pyun & Wang (2016 working paper, 'Implied Variance and Market Index Reversal'): the S&P 500 index, its futures and SPY show strong daily return reversal when implied variance (VIX) is high; mostly after NEGATIVE returns (positive returns weakly continue when IV is high); reversal is strongest for prices around the close and just after the open, and returns of the last 20-60 minutes reverse over the overnight + first 30 minutes. Similar in both halves of the sample. Their main evidence is variance-ratio / serial-covariance regressions, not a tradable rule, and they note the serial covariance 'generally takes longer than a day to resolve', i.e. a one-session hold captures only part of it.

Nagel (2012, RFS 25(7) 2005-2039), 'Evaporating Liquidity': short-term reversal returns proxy the return to liquidity provision; expected reversal returns rise strongly with VIX. Daily cross-sectional equities, not index futures.

prior: Weak, and LOW POWER even if the effect is real. A daily AR of about -0.02 to -0.08 implies a gross edge of a few hundredths of R on an open-to-close leg, at or below the 0.069R MES cost. With 300-600 trades the SE of mean R is ~0.04-0.05R, so side-matched twin p < 0.005 needs roughly +0.1R net: the chance of passing is low. Further: much of Jones et al.'s reversal is overnight / first 30 minutes (partly missed by a 09:35 entry) and takes longer than a day; it is concentrated after down days in high-IV regimes, which this symmetric unconditional rule does not target (no VIX feature, to stay within 3 features and 3 configs). The closed overnight close-auction fade is mild evidence against the overnight leg, not against this RTH leg.

mechanical_differences: Signal: shock_fade = one 5-minute bar's move mid-session (10:00-15:15) scaled by same-slot 5m volatility; D1 = the prior 1 or 5 full RTH sessions' close-to-close return scaled by 20-day DAILY return volatility. No intraday bar enters the D1 signal.

Timing: shock_fade enters intraday right after the shock bar, any time of day, possibly several times per session; D1 enters once per session at the 09:35 open, after the overnight session has passed.
Holding: shock_fade 30-minute time stop; D1 holds the full session to 15:55 or the bracket.
Bracket: shock_fade risk = the shock size (3+ pts, often tiny, cost 0.12-0.22R); D1 risk = 0.5 x ATR20 of daily true ranges (cost ~0.069R).

Horizon of the documented effect: shock_fade relied on intraday reversal at the open (Grant et al.) applied mid-session; D1 relies on daily-horizon index serial dependence (Baltussen et al.), a different anomaly in the literature.
overlap_with_closed.shared: Both are 'fade a large past move' reversal ideas and share the liquidity-provision story and the short_term_reversal tag; ES dev 2011-18 was already used by shock_fade as discovery (not one_look), so the multiple-testing disclosure counts it.

timestamp_semantics: bar['hist'] holds only sessions strictly before today (frozen eval, tests); 'ret' is the same-contract close-to-close return, roll-adjusted with the Globex switch gap measured before 09:30. The decision is taken on slot 0's close only because the engine acts on bar closes; the slot 0 close is used only as the bracket centre.
features: R_L = product over the last L hist entries (hist[-L:]) of (1 + ret) - 1 (L = 1 or 5); if any of them has ret None or nyse_skipped > 0, no signal
sd20 = sample sd (n-1) of ret over the entries of hist[-20:] (the last 20 hist entries ONLY, never further back) that have ret not None and nyse_skipped == 0; needs >= 18 such entries, else no signal
Half-day sessions in hist COUNT in R_L and sd20 exactly as recorded (their close-to-close ret is a real prior-close quantity); only TODAY being a half day skips the trade

rules.bars: 5m RTH bars; decision on slot 0's close (09:35), market fill at the next bar's open (09:35); the engine then manages the bracket.
rules.sessions: skip NYSE half days; skip sessions where ATR20(tr) over the last 20 hist entries is not computable (controller rule).
rules.entry: if |z| >= Z: side = -sign(z) (prior up-move -> short; down-move -> long). One trade per session at most.
rules.risk: stop = c0 - side * k * ATR20, target = c0 + side * k * ATR20, c0 = slot 0 close, ATR20 = mean of the last 20 hist 'tr' (roll-adjusted true range), k = 0.5. Controller-enforced.
rules.exit: stop, target, or the engine's flat at the 15:55 open.
rules.stale_prior_session: Accepted explicitly, not filtered: if the DATA lacks a scheduled NYSE day between hist[-1] and today (Databento gaps), hist[-1] is not yesterday and R_1 is stale. The strategy cannot see today's own gap count (nyse_skipped is only on hist entries) and has no date arithmetic. In ES dev this hits 3 trade sessions: 2014-06-16 (after 06-12/13), 2014-09-26 (after 09-23..25), 2015-01-02 (after 12-31). The run report lists whether any of them traded.
